description.narrative:
The general purpose of the second phase of the inclusive market project will be to enhance the i) to intensification of agroecological agriculture, ii) conscious use and consumption of resources and products and iii) social inclusion of the vulnerable population, of agri-food systems.
This will be done through 6 specific objectives:
- To facilitate access to international and national markets for agri-food products, promoting conscious food consumption.
- To facilitate the access of family productive units to adequate and innovative services, inputs, technology, and capacities for the intensification of agroecological agriculture and the efficient and sustainable use of resources.
- To promote the financial inclusion of men and women through i) access to microcredits and other forms of financing, ii) microinsurance for risk transfer and iii) financial education.
- To strengthen the capability of public and private institutions to support the economic, social, and environmental resilience of the target group
- To strengthen access to resources, services, and opportunities to expand capacities and skills that contribute to the empowerment of women and inclusion
- To enhance access to information, knowledge and systematized experiences on mechanisms, approaches, tools, methodologies, and others that contribute to advocacy on the issues prioritized by the project.

Det allmänna syftet med den andra fasen av det inkluderande marknadsprojektet är att påverka: i) intensifieringen av agroekologiskt jordbruk, ii) medveten användning och konsumtion av resurser och produkter och iii) social integration av den utsatta befolkningen inom agro-livsmedelssystem.

description.narrative:
During this period, 3,670 families of small-scale producers and harvesters distributed across the Chiquitanía, Amazon, and Valles Cruceños regions have increased their household income as a result of implementing sustainable production models and incorporating commercial innovations aimed at conserving natural resources.
Regarding its support in the promotion of Forest-Based Production Development Models. Swisscontact has supported the strengthening of value chains for Chiquitana almond, guapurú, isotoubo, açaí, and Brazil nut, with targeted support in the transformation and commercialization stages for national and international markets, and promotion of conscious consumption. In partnership with CEPAC, PROCESO, and FCBC, eight local enterprises collaborated with four allied SMEs (BIOFOOD, ALTERNATIVE FOODS, FRUELO, and A&E Laboratories) to supply forest products: Chiquitana almond, guapurú, cusi oil, and pesoé. By May 2025, these local enterprises had achieved sales totaling Bs.190,776, also promoted as part of the Chiquitano forest product basket Jasayé Chiquitano. Concerning agrobiodiversity products from the northern Amazon of La Paz (Palos Blancos and Alto Beni), six local enterprises partnered with BIOFOOD and ALTERNATIVE FOODS to sell banana flour and with the cooperative El Ceibo to supply dehydrated banana, achieving sales of Bs.1,388,860. Additionally, 17 tons of sustainable coffee from indigenous communities in the Amazon region of La Paz were exported to European and Nordic markets through the Danish company KAFFE LARS via the SME Chomateo, generating revenue of USD 118,000.
For sustainable agricultural production models, sustainable production practices were applied to 30,943 hectares of agricultural and pastoral ecosystems in the Chiquitanía and Valles Cruceños. Most of this area (26,443 hectares in agricultural systems and 4,500 hectares in pastoral systems) belongs to large and medium-scale producersincluding Mennonite groupswho cultivate at scale in the Chiquitanía. An 87% reduction in emissions was achieved in the intervention area by replacing 39,000 liters and/or kilos of chemical inputs with biological inputs. In the Valles Cruceños, sustainable management practices were introduced on 927 hectares of agricultural ecosystems, mainly in plots of small-scale producers of tomato, potato, vegetables, and beans.
Currently, 1,737 producers (960 men and 777 women) in the valleys of Santa Cruz (buffer zones) are applying sustainable management practices, primarily through reducing chemical inputs and using cultural practices for pest control. 1,571 producers (685 men and 886 women) in the Chiquitanía are applying sustainable practices (organic agriculture, sustainable farming and livestock practices).
For sustainable livestock production models, methane emissions were reduced by 13% in livestock areas using probiotics in cattle. Efforts were made to transition toward sustainable livestock practices with medium and large-scale producers in the Chiquitanía and Santa Cruz valleys. Collaborations promoted pasture recovery through biological inputs such as bio stimulants and biopesticides, as well as the use of probiotics and biological dewormers. These practices led to an 86% increase in pasture yield and number of harvests per year, improved animal health and productivity (both meat and milk), and reduced methane emissions.
In the Chiquitanía, the use of probiotics led to notable improvements in cattle health, including a 20% reduction in gastrointestinal diseases and weight gain of up to 2 kg in calves over 30 days. In the valleys, calves that received probiotics gained up to 7.8 kg in 2.5 months, compared to those without treatment. Additionally, milk production increased to 1.02 liters per cow per day. Finally, 1,519 women have improved their livelihoods as a result of adopting sustainable practices or measures to increase resilience to climate change.
